meta.label: Glasses and contact lenses
tradeoffLabels: easiest to buy without a store visit
meta.attribution: Covers prescription glasses and contact lenses bought in the US: online-only eyewear and contact lens sellers, in-store optical chains (several of which also sell online), two warehouse clubs, an independent-optometrist network, a nonprofit voucher programme, Medicaid coverage as a public route for people who qualify, and the free option of continuing to wear glasses that still match your prescription. Several chains share owners: EssilorLuxottica owns LensCrafters, Pearle Vision and Target Optical, and National Vision owns America's Best and Eyeglass World, as their own filings and pages state. Prices here are not perfectly comparable to each other. Some are a single frame's starting price, with lenses priced separately at checkout once a prescription is entered; some are a confirmed complete price for one pair, lenses included; some are a two-pair bundle; and contact lens prices are given per box or as a seller's own annual estimate, because how many boxes a year someone needs depends on the lens type and prescription. Each note says exactly what was confirmed on the page read and what was not. Every seller listed asks for prescription details before completing an order; none of these scores says anything about the quality of anyone's eyesight, only about price and how the product can be bought. Not medical advice; the American Optometric Association's own schedule for eye exam frequency is cited below for people deciding whether a new pair is needed at all. Reviewed 2026-08; expanded 2026-10, where some retailer pages could only be read in a rendered browser, as the notes say. The FTC's guide to your right to a copy of your prescription is linked from the online sellers. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Price for a pair of glasses or a box of contact lenses
States its price online, without a store visit or quote

products.name: Zenni Optical

economical.note: Zenni's own frame-price help page lists frames starting at $6.95, and states that this starting price reflects the frame itself, while adding lenses or protective coatings may add to the cost depending on the prescription. So $6.95 is a starting frame price, not a confirmed complete-pair total.

accessibility.note: Zenni sells online only and ships nationwide, with no membership fee, but the order process requires entering an existing prescription; no eye exam is offered.

transparency.note: Zenni publishes exact frame prices on its own site, including a page of frames all priced at $6.95.

products.description: An online-only eyewear seller with frames starting at $6.95, among the cheapest confirmed starting prices in this roster (Payne Glasses advertises $5.95), though lens cost is calculated separately once a prescription is entered.

products.name: Payne Glasses

economical.note: Payne Glasses' own homepage advertises '$5.95 Glasses' across its men's, women's and kids' categories, alongside a separate 'FREE Frames' promotion. The homepage does not show a single confirmed complete-pair total including lenses.

accessibility.note: Payne Glasses sells online only, with free shipping over $89 stated on the homepage, no membership fee, and no eye exam offered.

transparency.note: Payne Glasses states its $5.95 frame price directly on its own homepage.

products.description: An online-only eyewear seller advertising $5.95 frames, the lowest headline number in this roster, with lens cost added separately.

products.name: GlassesUSA (glasses)

economical.note: GlassesUSA's own homepage states glasses are 'Starting at just $19' in its 'Glasses on sale' section. The homepage does not confirm whether this starting price includes single-vision lenses.

accessibility.note: GlassesUSA sells online only, ships nationwide, with no membership fee and no eye exam offered; a prescription is entered during ordering.

transparency.note: GlassesUSA states a starting price directly on its own homepage.

products.description: An online-only eyewear seller advertising glasses starting at $19, the highest of the three online frame-only starting prices in this roster.

products.name: GlassesUSA (contact lenses)

economical.note: GlassesUSA's own contact lens page states 'someone with a standard prescription should pay somewhere between $250-$550 for a year's worth of contacts', its own estimate rather than a single box price, since cost depends on lens type and how many boxes a year the prescription needs.

accessibility.note: GlassesUSA sells contact lenses online with no membership fee; prescription information is required to complete an order.

transparency.note: GlassesUSA discloses a cost estimate for a year's supply directly on its own contact lens page, rather than requiring a store visit for a quote, though it does not show an exact box price on that page.

products.description: GlassesUSA's own estimate for a year of contact lenses on a standard prescription, priced as a range rather than a single box, sold online with no membership fee.

products.name: Eyeconic

economical.note: Eyeconic's own homepage states 'High-quality glasses in trendy shapes and colors from $139. Yes, that price includes your prescription lenses,' a confirmed complete-pair price including lenses, the highest confirmed complete single-pair price in this roster.

accessibility.note: Eyeconic sells online, and its homepage states VSP vision insurance is optional: 'No coverage? Ask your employer or check out a VSP Individual Vision Plan,' with a further 20 per cent off for people who do have VSP benefits linked. No physical visit is required to buy.

transparency.note: Eyeconic states its $139 complete price, including prescription lenses, directly on its own homepage, describing its pricing as 'what you see is what you pay.'

products.description: VSP's online eyewear seller, with a confirmed complete price of $139 including prescription lenses, usable with or without VSP vision insurance.

products.name: Stanton Optical

economical.note: Stanton Optical's own homepage advertises a '2-Pair Bundle, $79, FREE Eye Exam, FREE Single-Vision Lenses,' a confirmed complete price for two pairs including the exam and lenses, about $39.50 per pair.

accessibility.note: Stanton Optical requires an in-person store visit, but the eye exam is included free with the bundle rather than needing a separate appointment or fee, and the chain has locations nationwide.

transparency.note: Stanton Optical states its $79 two-pair bundle price directly on its own homepage.

products.description: An in-store optical chain advertising two complete pairs with a free eye exam for $79, the cheapest confirmed complete price per pair in this roster, but requiring a store visit.

products.name: MyEyeDr

economical.note: MyEyeDr's own homepage states 'Get a Complete Pair for Just $95' and 'Designer frames for just $169. Complete pairs for $95,' a confirmed complete price for one pair, higher per pair than the two-pair bundles offered by America's Best and Stanton Optical.

accessibility.note: MyEyeDr requires an in-person store visit; its homepage promotes savings through vision insurance ('Vision insurance covers your eye exam!') rather than stating a free exam is included without insurance.

transparency.note: MyEyeDr states its $95 complete-pair price directly on its own homepage.

products.description: An in-store optical chain with a confirmed complete price of $95 for one pair, the most expensive confirmed complete single-pair price in the in-store part of this roster, and an eye exam that its own homepage ties to insurance coverage rather than stating it is free.

products.name: America's Best (glasses)

economical.note: America's Best's own offer page states '2 PAIRS OF GLASSES + EYE EXAM FOR $95,' and that this 'includes single-vision, uncoated plastic lenses, frames tagged at $79.95, and a free eye exam,' a confirmed complete price for two pairs plus the exam, about $47.50 per pair. Upgrades to frames, coatings or lens types cost more, and the offer cannot be combined with insurance.

accessibility.note: America's Best requires an in-person store visit for this offer, but the comprehensive eye exam is included at no extra cost rather than needing a separate paid visit; exams without the two-pair purchase are $80 on their own.

transparency.note: America's Best states its $95 two-pair-plus-exam price directly on its own offer page.

products.description: A budget in-store chain bundling two complete pairs of single-vision glasses with a free eye exam for $95, requiring a store visit.

products.name: America's Best (contact lenses)

economical.note: America's Best's own contact lens page lists box prices including 'As low as $56.69 / $62.99 /box' for Sofmed Breathables XW and 'As low as $38.69 / $42.99 /box' for Sofmed Advanced, its own store-brand lenses; a separate 30 per cent off coupon code is offered for eyeglasses on the same page.

accessibility.note: America's Best sells contact lenses with prices and a filter tool shown directly on its own website; a valid prescription is required to complete an order.

transparency.note: America's Best publishes exact box prices for individual contact lens products directly on its own site.

products.description: America's Best's own store-brand contact lenses, with per-box prices published on its site starting near $38.69 for its cheapest listed lens.

products.name: Costco Optical

accessibility.note: Costco's own online eyeglasses FAQ states an active Costco membership and a Costco.com account are required to order, that Costco.com currently offers only single-vision and non-prescription lenses, and that bifocal, progressive or 'BAL' lenses can only be ordered through the Optical Department inside a physical warehouse.

transparency.note: Costco's own online eyeglasses FAQ does not state a price or price range anywhere on the page.

products.description: Costco's optical department, open only to paying Costco members; its own FAQ page does not publish a price, and full lens options require a warehouse visit rather than online ordering. A checkable price was not found on the pages read for this decision, so it is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Independent optometrist (Vision Source network)

accessibility.note: Vision Source describes itself on its own homepage as a 'Premier Network of Independent Optometrists,' directing visitors to find a local doctor; buying glasses or contacts this way always means an in-person visit to that practice rather than an online order.

transparency.note: Vision Source's own homepage contains no price, cost range or fee information for any practice in its network.

products.description: A local independent optometrist, represented here by the Vision Source network; price varies by practice and is not published centrally, and buying this way always means an in-person visit. A checkable price was not found for this decision, so it is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: New Eyes voucher programme

economical.note: New Eyes' own site describes 'Providing new prescription eyeglasses and clear vision to over 500,000 financially struggling children and adults across the United States' through a voucher system, at no cost to the qualifying recipient.

accessibility.note: New Eyes' own site describes helping people whose 'family can't afford to buy glasses' and references an application and voucher process, meaning this route requires demonstrating financial need and applying rather than being available to any shopper on demand; the site did not state specific income thresholds on the page read.

products.description: A US nonprofit that provides prescription eyeglasses at no cost through a voucher system to people who show financial need, rather than to any shopper who asks.

products.name: Keep wearing your current glasses

economical.note: No product to buy, so no cost, as long as the existing prescription still matches the eyes it was written for.

accessibility.note: NIH's National Eye Institute states how often a dilated eye exam is needed depends on individual risk, giving examples such as every one to two years for people over 60 or with a family history of glaucoma, and at least once a year for people with diabetes or high blood pressure. The American Optometric Association's own recommended schedule for asymptomatic, low-risk adults is 'at least every two years' for ages 18 to 64, and 'annually' from 65. Between exams, a person whose vision has not changed can keep wearing glasses they already own.

links.label: NIH National Eye Institute, dilated eye exam frequency
American Optometric Association, eye exam frequency

products.description: Continuing to wear glasses that still match a person's prescription, which the American Optometric Association's own exam schedule implies is reasonable between recommended checkups, at no cost at all.

products.name: Warby Parker (glasses)

economical.note: Warby Parker's own eyeglasses page states frames are starting at $95, including prescription lenses with scratch-resistant, anti-reflective coatings, and lists most frames at $95 with some at $175. A confirmed complete single-pair price, about the same as MyEyeDr's $95 complete pair. The page was read in a rendered browser because the site blocks plain downloads.

accessibility.note: Warby Parker's annual report on Form 10-K for 2025, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in February 2026, describes an omnichannel business across digital commerce and 323 retail stores in the US and Canada as of 31 December 2025, 285 of which offered in-person eye exams, plus a Virtual Vision Test for renewing a prescription. So glasses can be bought online with an existing prescription or in a store with an exam. The company's own eyeglasses page now carries a question about why it is ending its Home Try-On programme, so trying frames at home before buying should not be assumed.

transparency.note: Warby Parker states the $95 complete price, including prescription lenses, on its own eyeglasses page and shows each frame's price in the listing, without a store visit or quote.

links.label: FTC: your right to a copy of your prescription

products.description: An eyewear company that sells online and through about 320 stores, most with eye exams, with complete pairs including prescription lenses from $95.

products.name: LensCrafters

economical.note: LensCrafters' own homepage lists a 'Great value package' with 'Frame + lenses starting at $99', a starting complete-pair price; most of its other offers on the same page are percentage discounts (for example 40% off prescription glasses) rather than prices. Scored just below MyEyeDr's $95 complete pair.

accessibility.note: LensCrafters' own homepage says it accepts insurance 'both online and at our 1000+ locations across North America', offers shopping online with collection in store, free in-store fitting and adjustment, and booking an eye exam online. It is owned by EssilorLuxottica, which lists LensCrafters among its North American store banners. Pages beyond the homepage refused automated reading, so the return policy was not checked.

transparency.note: LensCrafters states a $99 starting price for frame plus lenses on its own homepage, but most of its savings are stated as percentages off prices that are only seen once a frame and lens options are chosen, and it promotes an 'In store quotation' service.

products.description: A large in-store optical chain owned by EssilorLuxottica, with 1,000+ locations and online ordering; frame and lenses start at $99, though most offers are percentage discounts.

products.name: Target Optical

economical.note: Target Optical's own special-offers page advertises 'Prescription glasses starting at $79' and refers to a '$79 frame and lens package offer', a confirmed starting complete-pair price for one pair; kids' prescription glasses start at $59. Upgrades and designer frames cost more (best-sellers are shown at $169 to $309 including lenses).

accessibility.note: Target Optical's own shipping and returns page lists free standard shipping, free ship-to-store, prescription eyewear processing of 1 to 8 business days plus shipping, and 'Free 90-Day Returns'. Its homepage says you can shop online from anywhere or at store locations, with eye exams from independent optometrists at or next to the stores. It is owned by EssilorLuxottica.

transparency.note: Target Optical states its $79 frame-and-lens package and per-frame prices including lenses on its own site, without a store visit; some offers are percentage discounts with exclusions.

products.description: An optical chain inside Target stores, owned by EssilorLuxottica, with online ordering, 90-day returns and complete pairs starting at $79.

products.name: Pearle Vision

accessibility.note: EssilorLuxottica, which owns Pearle Vision, lists it among its brick-and-mortar retail banners in North America. Pearle's own homepage (linked) says it has over 500 locations in the US, Canada and Puerto Rico and invites visitors to explore eyewear available in stores; no online checkout for glasses was found. Buying here means an in-person visit, with eye exams by independent optometrists at or next to its locations (or doctors employed by Pearle in some states).

transparency.note: Pearle Vision's own current promotions page lists offers only as percentages, such as '40% off lenses with frame purchase', with no frame, lens or complete-pair price. Its homepage gives only a general range for eye exam costs (about $50 to $200 without insurance) rather than its own prices.

products.description: A franchised in-store optical chain owned by EssilorLuxottica, with 500+ locations; it publishes discounts as percentages, not prices, so price is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Walmart Vision Center

economical.note: Walmart's own product page for its store-brand WM200650-1 women's frame showed $68.00 for the frame, with prescription lenses added at checkout from $20 more, so a complete pair from about $88. This is one example frame, not a confirmed cheapest price; Walmart's site blocks listing pages to automated readers, so the lowest frame price could not be checked. Read in a rendered browser.

accessibility.note: Walmart's own prescription glasses page explains ordering glasses online by selecting a frame and uploading a prescription, Vision Centers inside its stores, free in-store fittings and adjustments, an at-home vision test to renew a prescription, and returns online or in the app within 60 days. No membership is needed. Read in a rendered browser.

transparency.note: Walmart shows each frame's price and the starting price of lens options on its own product pages, without a store visit or quote.

links.label: Walmart prescription glasses and Vision Center
Walmart store-brand frame with lens pricing

products.description: Walmart's optical service, with Vision Centers in its stores and online ordering; an example store-brand frame plus basic prescription lenses came to about $88.

products.name: Sam's Club Optical

accessibility.note: Sam's Club's own Optical Center page answers in its FAQ that a valid membership and a valid prescription are needed to buy contact lenses or prescription eyewear, and that prescription glasses are bought at a local Sam's Club Optical Center (more than 500, it says). It offers a 60-day satisfaction guarantee on glasses. Membership and an in-club visit make this harder to use than an open online seller, similar to Costco. Read in a rendered browser.

transparency.note: Most frames on Sam's Club's own Optical Center page show a members-only price notice with a prompt to sign in instead of a price; one frame showed $89 to $149 with no statement of what lenses add. No complete-pair price was found without signing in.

products.description: Optical centres inside Sam's Club warehouses; a membership is required to buy, and most prices are shown only to signed-in members, so price is left out rather than guessed.

products.name: Visionworks

economical.note: Visionworks' own homepage says frames start at $79.99. That is a frame price only; lens prices were not stated on the pages read, so a complete pair costs more than $79.99 by an amount not shown. Scored a little below Eyeconic's confirmed $139 complete pair because the total is unconfirmed and the lowest frame price alone is already well above the online-only sellers' complete pairs. Read in a rendered browser.

accessibility.note: Visionworks' own guarantee page offers a 100-day guarantee: a complete pair can be returned for a refund or exchanged within 100 days of purchase. The site sells glasses and contacts online with free shipping and has stores with eye exams, but its homepage steers buyers to vision insurance, and most of its glasses offers are valid in store only. Read in a rendered browser.

transparency.note: Visionworks' own special-offers page states its discounts as percentages off list prices, and its small print says these are prices at which Visionworks may not actually have sold the frames and lenses. Only a frame starting price is stated on the homepage. Read in a rendered browser.

products.description: An in-store optical chain with a 100-day return guarantee; frames start at $79.99 before lenses, and most offers are percentages off list prices.

products.name: Eyeglass World

economical.note: Eyeglass World's own offer page advertises 2 pairs of glasses for $100, and states the offer includes single vision uncoated plastic (CR39) lenses and frames from its $100 price selection. A confirmed complete price of about $50 a pair, but unlike the America's Best $95 offer from the same owner, the eye exam is not included. Read in a rendered browser.

accessibility.note: National Vision's annual report on Form 10-K, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in March 2026, names Eyeglass World as one of its two owned brands alongside America's Best, and says Eyeglass World stores have on-site laboratories that can make some orders the same day. Eyeglass World's own site (linked) also sells glasses online with an existing prescription, with free shipping on online orders and a 30-day return policy.

transparency.note: Eyeglass World states its 2-for-$100 price and what it includes on its own offer page, without a store visit or quote.

products.description: A National Vision chain, sister to America's Best, selling two complete pairs for $100 (exam extra), with same-day lab service in some stores and online ordering.

products.name: 1-800 Contacts

economical.note: 1-800 Contacts' own AquaSoft Daily page says its store-brand daily lenses are just $25 per box and claims they are up to 40% cheaper than other daily lenses. The page does not state the box size, so a yearly cost was not worked out; branded lenses cost more. Daily lenses for both eyes typically cost several hundred dollars a year (Warby Parker's contacts page estimates $400 to $1,000). Read in a rendered browser.

accessibility.note: The FTC explains that you do not have to buy lenses from the eye doctor who examined you. If you don't give a seller a copy of your prescription, you can give them its details and the seller can check it with your doctor. 1-800 Contacts' own homepage (linked) offers exactly this: upload a photo of the prescription, type it in, or have them contact your doctor. It also offers an online vision exam to renew prescriptions, free standard shipping, and free returns of unopened boxes with no time limit.

transparency.note: 1-800 Contacts states a box price for its own lens on its own site; prices for other brands are shown on product pages that were not checked one by one.

links.label: FTC: buying glasses or contacts, your rights

products.description: A large online contact lens seller that can verify your prescription with your doctor and offers online renewals, with its own daily lens at $25 a box.

products.name: Hubble (contact lenses)

economical.note: Hubble's own homepage lists its Classic 2.0 Daily lenses at $29.99 per eye for a 30-pack, one month's supply, with a $1-per-eye starter pack and a first-order discount; other Hubble lenses cost $32.99 to $34.99 per eye per month at full price. At full price that is roughly $720 a year for both eyes on the cheapest daily, above GlassesUSA's own $250 to $550 annual estimate, though first-order discounts lower the first months.

accessibility.note: The FTC explains that a contact lens seller may verify your prescription with your doctor instead of requiring a copy. Hubble's own homepage (linked) works this way: you enter your prescription, Hubble contacts your doctor, and lenses ship on a subscription. In January 2022 the FTC announced a $3.5 million settlement with Vision Path, the company doing business as Hubble, over alleged failures to properly verify prescriptions and alleged switching of prescribed brands to Hubble lenses; that is history, not a current finding, but buyers should check their lenses match what their doctor prescribed.

transparency.note: Hubble shows per-pack prices, introductory discounts and the subscription model on its own homepage, without a store visit or quote.

links.label: FTC consumer alert on Hubble's $3.5 million settlement (2022)
FTC: buying glasses or contacts, your rights

products.description: A direct-to-consumer contact lens subscription selling its own lenses; prices are clear, but at full price the yearly cost is high, and it settled FTC charges over prescription verification in 2022.

products.name: Medicaid vision coverage

economical.note: Medicaid.gov's cost-sharing page says out-of-pocket costs apply to Medicaid enrollees except those exempted by law and 'most are limited to nominal amounts'. It also says 'Exempted groups include children, terminally ill individuals, and individuals residing in an institution.' So glasses covered by Medicaid cost an enrollee nothing or a small copay. Scored just below the fully free options because a copay may apply.

accessibility.note: Medicaid.gov's benefits page lists 'Eyeglasses' under optional benefits, and says 'States may provide optional benefits if they choose', so adult coverage for glasses depends on the state. For children under 21, Medicaid.gov's EPSDT page (linked) says vision services for enrolled children include treatment for defects in vision, such as eyeglasses. Either way, you must first qualify for Medicaid on income and other rules, so this route is not open to every shopper.

products.description: Public health coverage for people with low incomes: it must cover glasses for enrolled children, while adult coverage for glasses varies by state.
